title: Google Quadruples Miami Office as Co-Founders Flee California's Billionaire Tax
excerpt: Alphabet has expanded its Miami presence to 55,000 square feet after Larry Page and Sergey Brin purchased nearly $240 million in South Florida real estate, part of a broader exodus of tech wealth from the Golden State.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Alphabet expanded its Miami office to 55,000 square feet, quadrupling its previous size.
  • Larry Page and Sergey Brin spent nearly $240 million on Miami real estate, influencing Google's expansion.
  • A California ballot measure could impose a 5% tax on billionaires, prompting tech wealth migration.
  • Google's Miami office, opened in 2016, remains small compared to its 10-million-square-foot headquarters.

From Satellite Office to Strategic Outpost

Google's parent company Alphabet has more than quadrupled its office space in Miami this year, Bloomberg reported, transforming a modest satellite presence into what appears to be a growing strategic hub. The company signed a lease this spring to add roughly 45,000 square feet to its existing 10,000-square-foot office in Miami's financial district, according to people familiar with the matter.

The expansion was driven in part by the real estate purchases of Google's co-founders in South Florida, Bloomberg reported. Larry Page, the world's second-richest person with a net worth of $257 billion according to Forbes, has spent $188 million on Miami properties over the past year, including a $101.5 million estate in the upscale Coconut Grove neighborhood. Sergey Brin, ranked third globally at $237 billion, purchased a $51 million waterfront home in Miami Beach.

"Sergey Brin, ranked third globally at $237 billion, purchased a $51 million waterfront home in Miami Beach."

The California Billionaire Tax Factor

The timing is not coincidental. Page and Brin are among the highest-profile exits from California ahead of a November midterm ballot measure that could impose a one-time 5% wealth tax on residents worth over $1 billion. The state has roughly 200 billionaires who would be affected.

The duo, who built their fortunes after creating Google as Stanford University graduate students in 1998, have been systematically cutting ties with California. Earlier this year, they terminated or relocated several limited liability companies out of the state. Brin was also linked to a $42 million mansion purchase on the Nevada side of Lake Tahoe.

Brin and former Google CEO Eric Schmidt have reportedly joined forces with other Silicon Valley moguls to create a pro-business organization positioned to lobby against the billionaire tax.

Miami's Growing Tech Gravity

Google's expansion fits a broader pattern. More than 74 companies relocated their headquarters to Florida between 2020 and 2025, more than any other state, according to a JLL report. Palantir and Trinity Investments are among the firms that moved headquarters to Miami in early 2026.

Both Google founders and Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg have spent tens of millions on Miami real estate this year, creating a gravitational pull that is drawing corporate investment and talent to South Florida. The state posted 10,522 new tech jobs last year — more than any other state besides Texas, according to CompTIA.

Google first opened a Miami office in 2016. While the expansion represents a significant percentage increase, the South Florida operation remains a fraction of the company's 10-million-square-foot Mountain View campus in California and its 1.7-million-square-foot Hudson Square campus in New York.

What It Signals for the Diaspora

For Indian professionals in tech, the Miami expansion represents another node in the diversifying geography of U.S. tech employment. While Silicon Valley and Seattle remain the industry's center of gravity, the growing presence of Google and other major employers in Florida could create new opportunities — and new visa sponsorship destinations — in a state with no personal income tax.

Page and Brin stepped down from executive roles in 2019 but remain on Alphabet's board and hold majority voting control. Brin has reportedly taken an active role in shaping the company's AI initiatives, making his proximity to any Google office operationally significant.

The broader billionaire migration from California also raises questions about the long-term tax base of a state that has been home to most major Indian-founded tech companies, from Google itself to Adobe, and about the political dynamics of wealth taxation that could eventually affect other high-net-worth diaspora entrepreneurs.
